column2: On the authority of Abū Muḥammad al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the grandson of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his sweet basil (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said:
I memorised from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: “Leave what gives you doubt for what does not give you doubt.” Reported by al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī; al-Tirmidhī said: An authentic (ṣaḥīḥ) hadith.
Sibṭ (“grandson”): the son of his daughter Fāṭimah. Wa-rayḥānatuhu (“and his sweet basil”): an expression of his love for him and delight in him.
Daʿ (“leave”): abandon. Yurībuka (“gives you doubt”): what you are uncertain about.
“For what does not give you doubt”: for what you are not uncertain about.
A Muslim should build his affairs on certainty, so that he is clear-sighted in the matter of his religion.
The prohibition of falling into doubtful matters and into that about which the soul wavers as to whether it is lawful or unlawful.
It is recommended to be scrupulous about anything in which there is a suspicion of unlawfulness, even if the basic ruling is that it is lawful.
This hadith guides us to the fact that the believer leaves what he doubts is lawful, for fear of falling into the unlawful without realising it. Rather, he should

move from what he doubts to what is certainly lawful, with no doubt in it, so that his heart is at ease and his soul at rest, desiring what is purely lawful and keeping far from the unlawful, the doubtful and that about which the soul wavers; and he should be as the poet said:
Matters and deeds have an outcome, / so fear a sudden recompense and beware of it in good time.
The man of sense leaves what he craves, fearing / a hateful remedy for the harm it brings.
It is part of manliness for a man to leave his craving; / so look to which of the two you have preferred, and take heed.
